trace.topic: What to Do If You’re An NRR Zombie
trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should define the NRR problem clearly: a company with weak expansion or unhealthy retention despite still appearing alive.
It should recommend concrete responses such as fixing product value, segmentation, onboarding, pricing, or customer success.
It should stress that weak NRR becomes a structural drag on growth.
rubric_must_haves: Defines the term in plain language.
Explains why the condition is dangerous.
Offers specific operational fixes rather than abstract encouragement.
Sounds direct and urgent without being melodramatic.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should explain that an 'NRR zombie' is a company that can still grow on the surface but lacks the expansion and retention engine needed for healthy compounding. The founder takeaway is to diagnose the root cause quickly and fix the product, segmentation, pricing, or customer outcomes before the weakness hardens into a permanent ceiling.

trace.answer: So we've talked before on SaaStr about how I call this the NRR Zombie. And what an NRR zombie looks like, and why you gotta watch out for them. But now let me ask you, have you noticed in the past few months there are just so many of 'em? That maybe we never had before. Because back when everyone was still growing, folks were hiding some bad stuff behind crazy high growth. So no one cared quite as much. We all sort of knew that if things got harder, we'd see who didn't really have happy customers. Now we know for sure. We've been doing these AI agents for years, but then GPT-4 came out and Claude came out, and these things just started getting better every single month. And today, you could literally train an agent using Claude Code to do deep dives on every account. This is going to change our world. So you're seeing it everywhere. You're seeing it with Zoom, you're seeing it with Slack, you're seeing it with HubSpot. They're all struggling. The founders are under pressure, their boards are under pressure, their employees are under stress. It's tough out here right now. But look, I get it. Even in the best of times, not every start-up grows perfectly. Not every company grows as fast as it should. There's always someone leaving. Someone new joining. It takes time to scale up sales teams. Sometimes you overhire. And sometimes it just gets harder. But during downturns, especially, we see this massive amount of churn. Why? Because renewal conversations become painful. Customers go through budget reviews where they decide they need to cut $300K out of software spend because prices went up too much. Or worse, price increases lead to downgrades.

retrieval_hits.text:
1. NRR is destiny.
When NRR drops below 110%, alarm bells should go off. Below 100%, you’re in serious trouble. Monitor this metric religiously.

#4.  Don’t settle for less growth than Your NRR + 20%
.
E.g., if your NRR is 120%, even if times are tougher, don’t settle for growing at least +40% next year. Don’t hide in excuses and a high NRR.  Don’t hide in renewals and in your CRO forcing the base to pay more.  Force yourself to at least grow +20% more than your NRR.

#4.  Don’t settle for less growth than Your NRR + 20%
.  E.g., if your NRR is 120%, even if times are tougher, don’t settle for growing at least +40% next year.  Not all your customer base has evaporated.  Don’t hide in excuses and a high NRR.  Don’t hide in renewals.  Don’t force your base to pay more than they want to.  Force yourself to at least grow +20% more than your NRR.

2. NRR is the canary in the coal mine.
Snowflake’s decline from 158% to 125% foreshadowed everything else. If your best customers aren’t expanding, you have a problem.
